Polymer-Attenuated Coulombic Self-Assembly (PACS) is a flexible experimental approach for generating crystals from simple colloidal building blocks. The central components are charged spherical particles coated with a polymer brush that prevents irreversible aggregation. Whether oppositely charged c…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 035423] Published Fri Sep 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a flexible simulation framework for polymer-attenuated Coulombic self-assembly of charged colloidal particles coated with polymer brushes.
motivation: Polymer-Attenuated Coulombic Self-Assembly (PACS) is an experimental approach for creating colloidal crystals from simple building blocks, and a simulation framework is needed to model and predict their assembly behavior.
method: The authors develop a simulation framework to study charged spherical particles with polymer brushes that prevent irreversible aggregation, focusing on the role of oppositely charged components.
result: The framework enables flexible simulation of PACS and likely provides insights into the conditions for crystal formation, though the abstract is truncated.
conclusion: The work offers a computational tool for understanding and designing colloidal self-assembly, primarily relevant to soft matter physics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Attraction-induced Cluster Fragmentation And Local Alignment In Active Particle Systems
authors: Sota Shimamura, Nen Saito, And Shuji Ishihara
abstract:
Author(s): Sota Shimamura, Nen Saito, and Shuji Ishihara

We numerically studied active Brownian particles with attractive interactions. Contrary to our intuition, the attractive force between particles disrupts the formation of a single cluster observed in motility-induced phase separation, giving rise to a multicluster state. This transition is driven by…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 035414] Published Mon Sep 14, 2026.
tldr: Numerical study showing that attractive interactions between active Brownian particles fragment a single motility-induced cluster into a multicluster state with local alignment.
motivation: Motility-induced phase separation normally produces a single macroscopic cluster, and the authors ask how attractive forces alter this collective behavior in active matter.
method: Active Brownian particles with attractive interactions are simulated numerically, characterizing cluster statistics and orientational ordering across parameter regimes.
result: Contrary to intuition, attraction disrupts the single-cluster state and drives a transition to a fragmented multicluster phase accompanied by local alignment of particle orientations.
conclusion: The work reveals a fragmentation mechanism in active matter with attraction, broadening the phenomenology of motility-induced phase separation.

title: Detecting Remote Synchronization From Empirical Data Of Brain Networks
authors: Dehua Chen, Zhiyin Yang, Zhaohua Lin, Guoshen Liang, Wenbin Mao, And Zonghua Liu
abstract:
Author(s): Dehua Chen, Zhiyin Yang, Zhaohua Lin, Guoshen Liang, Wenbin Mao, and Zonghua Liu

The emergence of functional connectivity between distant brain regions that lack a direct structural link remains a long-standing question in neuroscience. Remote synchronization (RS) offers a promising framework for uncovering the underlying mechanisms. So far, RS has been well studied in artificia…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033307] Published Mon Sep 14, 2026.
tldr: The paper develops a method to detect remote synchronization (RS) in empirical functional brain networks, identifying indirect synchronization between distant brain regions lacking direct structural connections.
motivation: The emergence of functional connectivity between physically unconnected brain regions remains unexplained in neuroscience, and remote synchronization provides a candidate mechanism, though prior work has focused mainly on artificial network models rather than real data.
method: The authors analyze empirical brain network data and apply synchronization-detection techniques to identify patterns of remote synchronization, examining how indirect coupling paths give rise to correlated dynamics between distant nodes.
result: Remote synchronization is detected in empirical brain network data, revealing that distant, structurally unconnected regions can synchronize via intermediate nodes, offering a mechanistic account of observed functional connectivity.
conclusion: Remote synchronization is a viable framework for explaining long-range functional connectivity in the brain, extending its study from artificial models to real empirical data.

title: Pitching Cosmic Curveballs: Environmental Effects On Extreme-Mass-Ratio Inspirals With Spinning Secondaries
authors: Leif Lui, Lisa V. Drummond, And Alejandro Torres-Orjuela
abstract:
Author(s): Leif Lui, Lisa V. Drummond, and Alejandro Torres-Orjuela

Much like the aerodynamic deflection of a spinning curveball, a rotating secondary in an extreme-mass-ratio inspiral (EMRI) experiences Magnus and lift forces, in addition to the standard drag force, when traversing a gaseous environment. We present the first framework that incorporates these specif…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 121403] Published Wed Sep 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework for modeling extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) with spinning secondaries in gaseous environments, including Magnus and lift forces beyond standard drag.
motivation: EMRIs are key gravitational-wave sources for LISA, and environmental interactions with gas can alter their orbital evolution and emitted waveforms, yet aerodynamic forces from a spinning secondary have been neglected.
method: The authors develop the first framework that incorporates Magnus and lift forces, in addition to drag, for a rotating secondary body traversing a gaseous medium during an EMRI.
result: The inclusion of these forces is shown to modify the inspiral trajectory and gravitational-wave signal, potentially affecting parameter estimation for future observations.
conclusion: Environmental effects from spinning secondaries should be included in EMRI waveform models to avoid biases in astrophysical inference.

title: Magnetic Turbulence Boosts Supernova Signals Of Axion-Photon Conversion
authors: Damiano F. G. Fiorillo, Ángel Gil Muyor, Georg G. Raffelt, And Edoardo Vitagliano
abstract:
Author(s): Damiano F. G. Fiorillo, Ángel Gil Muyor, Georg G. Raffelt, and Edoardo Vitagliano

Magnetic fields between a supernova (SN) and Earth convert axions into gamma rays. The absence of such a signal in coincidence with SN 1987A neutrinos, using the coherent Milky Way field, provides well-studied constraints on [MATH] (axion-proton times axion-photon couplings) and on ${g}…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 121002] Published Tue Sep 15, 2026.
tldr: Magnetic turbulence between a supernova and Earth can enhance axion-photon conversion signals, affecting constraints on axion couplings.
motivation: Axions may convert to gamma rays in cosmic magnetic fields, and the absence of a coincident gamma-ray signal from SN 1987A has been used to constrain axion couplings.
method: The authors analyze how magnetic turbulence in the Milky Way field modifies the coherent conversion probability for axions emitted by a supernova.
result: Turbulence can boost the expected gamma-ray signal, which weakens or alters the previously derived constraints on axion-proton and axion-photon couplings.
conclusion: Proper modeling of magnetic turbulence is necessary for reliable supernova axion constraints, and the revised bounds may be less stringent than earlier estimates.

title: Fastest First-Passage Time For Multiple Searchers With Finite Speed
authors: Denis S. Grebenkov, Ralf Metzler, And Gleb Oshanin
abstract:
Author(s): Denis S. Grebenkov, Ralf Metzler, and Gleb Oshanin

Classical first-passage theory based on Brownian motion predicts that the mean fastest-arrival time decreases only logarithmically with the number of searchers, however this is an artifact of the unphysical infinite-speed assumption of Brownian dynamics.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 127102] Published Tue Sep 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the fastest first-passage time for multiple classical searchers moving at finite speed, showing that the logarithmic scaling predicted by Brownian motion is an artifact of infinite-speed dynamics.
motivation: Classical first-passage theory based on Brownian motion predicts only logarithmic improvement with more searchers, but this relies on unphysical infinite-speed motion.
method: The authors analyze the mean fastest-arrival time for multiple searchers constrained to finite speed, likely using stochastic process theory and asymptotic analysis.
result: They find that finite-speed constraints change the scaling of the fastest first-passage time compared to the Brownian-motion prediction.
conclusion: The work clarifies how finite searcher speed alters classical search kinetics, with implications for understanding optimal search strategies in physical systems.

title: Aerosol Generation By The Splashing Of Low Viscosity Drops Impacting Liquid Layers
authors: Guillaume Riboux And José M. Gordillo
abstract:
Author(s): Guillaume Riboux and José M. Gordillo

Using theory and numerical simulations, here we describe the early stages of the impact with a velocity [MATH] of a drop of radius [MATH] of a low viscosity liquid such as water against a layer of generic thickness [MATH] of the same liquid. Our predictions for the initial velocity [MATH] and the …


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 124001] Published Mon Sep 14, 2026.
tldr: A theoretical and numerical study of the early-stage dynamics of low-viscosity drop impacts on liquid layers, focusing on splashing and aerosol generation.
motivation: Understanding how drops splash upon impacting liquid layers is important for predicting aerosol production in natural and industrial settings.
method: The authors combine analytical theory with numerical simulations to model the initial impact of a water drop of radius R hitting a layer of generic thickness h at velocity V.
result: Predictions are obtained for the initial velocity of the ejecta and the dynamics of the early impact stages, capturing the onset of splashing for low-viscosity liquids.
conclusion: The work clarifies the hydrodynamic mechanisms governing splash and aerosol formation in low-viscosity drop impacts on liquid films.

title: Fully Differential Photoionization Delays In The Water Molecule
authors: Prateek Pranjal, Jesus González-Vázquez, Fernando Martín, And Roger Y. Bello
abstract:
Author(s): Prateek Pranjal, Jesus González-Vázquez, Fernando Martín, and Roger Y. Bello

We present fully correlated calculations of angularly resolved one- and two-photon photoionization delays in [MATH] for different ionization channels and light-polarization directions. By solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation in full dimensionality, we obtain molecula…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 033109] Published Tue Sep 15, 2026.
tldr: The paper computes fully correlated angularly resolved one- and two-photon photoionization delays in the water molecule using time-dependent Schrödinger equation calculations.
motivation: Photoionization delays provide insight into attosecond electron dynamics and molecular photoionization processes, which are of interest in ultrafast AMO physics.
method: The authors solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation in full dimensionality to obtain molecular photoionization delays for different ionization channels and light-polarization directions.
result: Fully correlated calculations yield angularly resolved one- and two-photon photoionization delays for various channels in H2O.
conclusion: The work provides detailed theoretical predictions for attosecond photoionization delays in water, relevant to interpreting ultrafast spectroscopic experiments.

title: Uniform Asymptotic Theory Of The Secondary Rainbow: Regularization Of Polarization-dependent Caustics
authors: Zhenyu Wang, Yingchun Wu, And Xuecheng Wu
abstract:
Author(s): Zhenyu Wang, Yingchun Wu, and Xuecheng Wu

The secondary rainbow, a classic fold caustic, presents a long-standing challenge in wave theory because standard semiclassical approximations predict unphysical intensity nulls near the Brewster angle. We resolve this Brewster-caustic confluence by developing a uniform asymptotic theory that integr…


[Phys. Rev. A 114, 033516] Published Tue Sep 15, 2026.
tldr: The paper develops a uniform asymptotic theory for the secondary rainbow that resolves the Brewster-caustic confluence and eliminates unphysical intensity nulls.
motivation: Standard semiclassical approximations fail near the Brewster angle in the secondary rainbow, predicting unphysical intensity nulls.
method: A uniform asymptotic theory is constructed to regularize polarization-dependent caustics associated with the fold caustic of the secondary rainbow.
result: The theory removes the unphysical intensity nulls and yields a correct description of the secondary rainbow's intensity pattern near the Brewster angle.
conclusion: The work advances the wave theory of optical caustics but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Local Elastic Perturbation Of Colloidal Suspensions Near The Colloidal Glass Transition
authors: Piotr Habdas, Rachel E. Courtland, And Eric R. Weeks

[Phys. Rev. E 114, 035422] Published Fri Sep 18, 2026.
tldr: An experimental study of local elastic perturbations in dense colloidal suspensions near the colloidal glass transition using a rotating magnetic probe and confocal microscopy.
motivation: To understand the mechanical response and local dynamics of colloidal glasses under external perturbations, which is important in soft matter physics.
method: Isolated magnetic probe particles are rotated by an external magnet to induce local perturbations, and confocal microscopy tracks both the probe and adjacent colloidal particles.
result: The probe moves on a circular trajectory, and the surrounding particles exhibit elastic-like displacements that reveal heterogeneous dynamics near the glass transition.
conclusion: The work provides insights into local elasticity and flow in colloidal glasses, contributing to the broader understanding of glassy dynamics in soft materials.

title: Permeability Of Deforming Soft Particle Packs
authors: Jérémie Vasseur, Fabian B. Wadsworth, Jingwei Zhang, And Yan Lavallée
abstract:
Author(s): Jérémie Vasseur, Fabian B. Wadsworth, Jingwei Zhang, and Yan Lavallée

The permeability of the fluid between packs of particles is an important parameter for a range of natural and industrial applications. Here, we start from experiments in which soft spherical particles—“soft balls”—are compressed uniaxially, resulting in particle-particle flattening and an overall de…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 035424] Published Fri Sep 18, 2026.
tldr: Experimental and modeling study of how uniaxial compression and particle flattening affect fluid permeability in packs of soft spherical particles.
motivation: Permeability of particle packs is important for natural and industrial processes, but the effect of particle deformation on permeability is not well understood.
method: Soft spherical particles are compressed uniaxially, causing particle-particle flattening, and the resulting permeability is measured and analyzed.
result: The experiments reveal how deformation and flattening alter the pore structure and thus the permeability of the pack.
conclusion: The findings provide a better understanding of permeability in deforming soft particle systems relevant to geophysical and industrial applications.

title: Dominance Switching Between Substrate Adhesion And Curvature In Directional Collective Cell Migration
authors: Bing Qi, Jianwen Li, Xinxin Lv, Xi-Qiao Feng, And Jing Du
abstract:
Author(s): Bing Qi, Jianwen Li, Xinxin Lv, Xi-Qiao Feng, and Jing Du

Substrate curvature and cell-substrate adhesion are two key physical determinants of directional collective cell migration, yet their joint regulatory mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we establish a physical framework based on the instantaneous force balance to reveal the dominance switching mech…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 034406] Published Thu Sep 17, 2026.
tldr: The paper develops a physical framework based on instantaneous force balance to explain how substrate curvature and cell-substrate adhesion alternately dominate during directional collective cell migration.
motivation: Substrate curvature and cell-substrate adhesion are both known to influence collective cell migration, but how they jointly regulate directional migration remained unclear.
method: A force-balance physical framework is constructed to model the competition between substrate adhesion and curvature effects in migrating cell collectives.
result: The analysis reveals a dominance-switching mechanism in which adhesion or curvature governs the migration direction depending on the balance of instantaneous forces.
conclusion: The framework unifies two key physical determinants of collective cell migration and predicts when each factor dominates, offering a quantitative model for tissue biophysics.

title: State Space Navigation Using Geometrically Symmetric Inflatables
authors: Brent Michiels, Elias de Smet, And Benjamin Gorissen

tldr: The paper explores how geometrically symmetric inflatable soft actuators can be used for state-space navigation and embodied computation.
motivation: Soft robots lack embodied computation and memory of past events because inflatable actuators typically relax once pressure is removed, limiting autonomous complex functionality.
method: The authors design and analyze geometrically symmetric inflatable structures to navigate a state space, likely using physical experiments and modeling of their nonlinear response.
result: The inflatables exhibit state-dependent behavior that enables navigation through a state space, providing a form of embodied computation and information storage.
conclusion: Geometrically symmetric inflatables offer a promising route to soft robotic control and memory, though the work is entirely outside quantum information science.

This study is motivated by the recent radar detection of liquid water underneath the M…


[Phys. Rev. E 114, 035416] Published Tue Sep 15, 2026.
tldr: Molecular dynamics simulations reveal slow glassy dynamics and a fragile-to-strong crossover in supercooled aqueous magnesium perchlorate solutions relevant to Martian conditions.
motivation: Motivated by radar detection of liquid water beneath the Martian south polar ice cap, the study aims to understand the dynamical behavior of water in magnesium perchlorate solutions under supercooled conditions.
method: Classical molecular dynamics simulations using the TIP4P/2005 water model and the extended Madrid-2019 force field were performed for aqueous magnesium perchlorate solutions.
result: The simulations show slow glassy dynamics and a fragile-to-strong crossover in the supercooled regime, highlighting the influence of Martian solutes on water dynamics.
conclusion: The findings provide insight into the physical properties of potential Martian brines and demonstrate the utility of molecular dynamics for planetary relevant aqueous solutions.

motivation: Understanding the transmembrane voltage in nanoporous membranes is important for optimizing desalination and blue-energy harvesting, as well as for physiological ion channels.
method: The authors likely employ theoretical modeling and possibly simulations of ion transport in charged nanochannels subject to salinity gradients to derive expressions for the zero-current potential.
result: The work characterizes how the transmembrane potential depends on channel charge, salinity gradient, and geometry, providing a framework for predicting ionic current nullification conditions.
conclusion: The findings advance the modeling of electrokinetic transport in nanochannels and may inform the design of efficient membrane-based energy and desalination systems.

motivation: Chimera states are intriguing but their reliable identification remains challenging despite extensive study in nonlinear dynamics.

result: The method is demonstrated to reliably detect chimera states across different settings, improving upon existing identification approaches.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for studying chimera states, but it falls outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

motivation: Multilevel sociality, where large communities emerge from interconnected subgroups, is a hallmark of primate societies and central to the social brain hypothesis, motivating the question of whether such organization alone can foster cooperation.
method: The authors presumably use evolutionary game theory and network models to analyze cooperation dynamics in community-structured populations where defection is individually advantageous.
result: They find that community structure can enable contagious cooperation, suggesting that organizational forms can sustain cooperative behavior despite individual incentives to defect.
conclusion: The work implies that multilevel social organization may play a key role in the evolution of cooperation, independent of other mechanisms.

method: The authors likely use experiments and/or simulations to investigate how particle size, friction, restitution, and cohesion influence the percolation and trapping of fines in a static bed.
result: Cohesive fines exhibit percolation behavior distinct from noncohesive fines, with cohesion playing a significant role in determining whether particles pass through or become trapped.
conclusion: Cohesion is a key factor controlling fine-particle percolation in static beds, with implications for industrial and natural granular systems.

In active matter and living matter, such as clusters of migrating cells, collective dynamics emerges from the underlying interactions. A common assumption of theoretical descriptions of collective cell migration is that these interactions are pairwise additive. It remains unclear, however, whether t…

tldr: This paper investigates whether three-body (higher-order) interactions, rather than pairwise-additive forces, are needed to explain collective dynamics in migrating cell clusters.
motivation: Theoretical models of collective cell migration typically assume pairwise-additive interactions, but it is unclear whether this assumption is valid for dense, interacting cell clusters.
method: The authors analyze cell migration data and use inference/modeling techniques to test pairwise versus three-body interaction descriptions of the collective dynamics.
result: The analysis indicates that three-body interactions are required to accurately capture the observed collective migration behavior, challenging purely pairwise descriptions.
conclusion: Higher-order interactions are essential for describing collective cell migration, with implications for models of active and living matter.

motivation: Understanding how shear localization and particle alignment in nonspherical granular materials affect pressure distribution is important for granular physics and industrial applications.
method: The authors simulate or experimentally study a split-bottom shear cell filled with elongated grains, varying interparticle friction to analyze pressure differences and alignment.
result: A pressure difference develops within the sheared material, with high friction leading to increased alignment and stronger shear localization.
conclusion: Interparticle friction controls the coupling between shear localization, particle alignment, and pressure heterogeneity in granular materials of nonspherical particles.

conclusion: The proposed ponderomotive achromat offers a new approach to aberration correction in electron optics, though it lies outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.
